1.title: Know the types of child care and what children need
1.intro: Child care takes many forms. First learn the words and what children need at each age.
pts: Name the types: licensed centre, licensed home care, unlicensed home care, nanny and babysitter.
Explain the basic needs of children: safety, food, rest, play, comfort and caring adults.
Describe broad age stages: baby, toddler, preschool and school age.
Explain that children learn through play, routine and kind talk.
Say what a carer does not do: give medical care beyond first aid or replace parents.
Compare the day of a toddler with the day of a school-age child and list how their needs differ.
List questions a parent may ask a carer on a first visit.
1.ex: A toddler cries when a parent leaves. A carer greets the child by name, offers a favourite toy, keeps a calm voice and tells the parent the child settled after ten minutes. The daily note adds that the child napped 60 minutes and ate half of the snack.
1.act: Write a one-page glossary of ten terms and describe the needs of one age group.
1.std: Task: define terms and needs. Condition: one page, own words. Standard: each term is correct and needs match the age group.

2.title: Know the rules and licensing
2.intro: Child care rules are set by each province. Know which type of care needs a licence.
pts: Explain that licensing, number of children per carer and training are set by provinces and territories; check the current rule with the provincial child care authority.
Explain that unlicensed care is often limited to a small number of children; check the exact limit locally.
Explain that background checks, including a vulnerable-sector check, are commonly required; check what applies.
Explain that you must report suspected abuse or neglect to the child protection authority; learn the local duty and the number to call.
Explain that child care fee support and space programmes differ by province; check the current rules.
Keep copies of your licence, training certificates and check results ready to show.
Write the phone number of the provincial child care authority in your file.
2.ex: A person wants to care for six children at home. Before starting she asks the provincial authority whether that needs a licence, and waits for the answer in writing. She does not start until she has it.
2.act: Make a rules table with rule, who enforces it, what you must do and a dated official source.
2.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: official pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a dated source; no rule is guessed.

3.title: Keep children safe and healthy
3.intro: Safety comes first. Prevent harm, and know what to do if something goes wrong.
pts: Never leave a child alone; keep the required ratio of adults to children.
Check rooms and toys for hazards such as small parts, cords, hot items and unlocked doors.
Follow safe sleep rules for babies; get the current guidance from the public health unit.
Wash hands before meals and after toilet, and clean toys and surfaces on a schedule.
Take first aid and CPR training that fits the ages you care for; keep it current.
Plan and practise fire and emergency drills with the children.
Use car seats and strollers as the maker's instructions say.
3.ex: Each morning a carer does a ten-point walk round: gates, plugs, cleaning products, floor, toys. One day she finds a loose button in the play area and removes it. If the walk takes 5 minutes a day, that is 5 x 5 = 25 minutes in a five-day week.
3.act: Create a safety checklist for a room and use it for a week.
3.std: Task: use a safety checklist. Condition: one week. Standard: every item is checked and dated and each hazard found is fixed and recorded.

4.title: Plan a day: routines, meals and play
4.intro: A calm routine helps children feel safe. Plan a day in small blocks.
pts: Plan blocks: arrival, play, snack, outdoor time, rest, lunch, quiet play, pick-up.
Offer play that fits the age: sensory play, building, stories, music, movement.
Ask parents about allergies and diets and post them where staff can see.
Follow food safety rules for storing and serving food; check local guidance.
Prepare for weather: spare clothes, sun cover in summer and warm gear in winter.
Warn children before a change, for example 'five minutes until tidy-up'.
Keep a rainy-day plan with indoor movement games.
4.ex: A day plan for 3-year-olds has 45 minutes of outdoor time in the morning, a story of 15 minutes, then lunch. Outdoor time and story together fill 45 + 15 = 60 minutes. A child with a nut allergy has a picture card at the lunch table.
4.act: Write a one-day plan with times, activities, meals and safety notes for one age group.
4.std: Task: plan a day. Condition: one age group. Standard: blocks fit age, allergies are posted and safety notes are included.

5.title: Guide behaviour and support learning
5.intro: Children learn from adults who are calm, clear and kind.
pts: Set a few clear rules in simple words and show what to do instead.
Notice good behaviour and name it.
Stay calm when a child is upset; get down to their level and name the feeling.
Never use hitting or shaming; follow the rules on discipline in your province.
Support early learning through talk, songs, counting and picture books.
Offer two choices so the child feels some control.
Give a calm result that fits the action, such as helping to tidy a mess, never a punishment.
5.ex: A child grabs a toy. The carer says 'Ask with words', models 'Can I have a turn?' and helps both children take turns of two minutes each. She notes it for the parent.
5.act: Practise three behaviour situations with a partner and write what you said.
5.std: Task: guide behaviour. Condition: three role-plays. Standard: language is calm and clear, no shaming is used and the child is shown what to do.

6.title: Talk with parents and keep records
6.intro: Parents trust you with what matters most. Talk often and write things down.
pts: Give a short daily note: food, sleep, play, mood and any incident.
Write an incident report the same day for any injury, with time, what happened and what you did.
Keep consent forms, emergency contacts, allergies and pick-up lists.
Protect children's privacy; never share photos or details without consent.
Meet families in English, French or another language where you can; use plain words.
Hold a short chat at drop-off to hear about changes at home.
Find out how long records must be kept; check the provincial rule.
6.ex: A child bumps his head. The carer applies first aid, writes a report with the time and treatment, tells the parent at pick-up and asks her to sign. The report is filed the same day with the signed copy.
6.act: Create a daily note, an incident form and a consent form.
6.std: Task: build family forms. Condition: plain words. Standard: forms cover who, what, when and signature, and keep private data safe.

7.title: Set fees and plan a small child care business
7.intro: A child care business must cover costs and follow the law. This is not financial advice; ask a licensed accountant.
pts: List costs: food, supplies, rent share, insurance, training, equipment, your time.
Fee per child per day = (monthly costs + target income) / (child-days you can fill).
Check what insurance is needed and whether the provincial authority sets fee rules; check locally.
Write a contract: hours, fees, late pick-up, sickness rules, holidays and notice.
Plan for empty spaces: you will not fill every day.
Write a sick-child policy that says when a child must stay home.
Track child-days filled each month and compare them with your plan.
7.ex: Monthly costs are 960 CAD and target income is 2,240 CAD, a total of 3,200. You can fill 160 child-days. Fee = 3,200 / 160 = 20 CAD per child per day. If only 140 days fill, income is 140 x 20 = 2,800, which is 400 short of the plan.
7.act: Build a cost sheet and a fee, and write a one-page family agreement.
7.std: Task: set a fee. Condition: a spreadsheet. Standard: costs are listed, the fee sum is correct and the agreement is clear.

8.title: Run a child care service for real
8.intro: Run it steadily: routines, safety, records and improving.
pts: Review safety checks, incident reports and attendance every week.
Ask parents for feedback each term and act on it.
Take part in training each year and keep certificates.
Look after yourself: breaks, backup carer and a plan for sick days.
Write a 12-month plan with milestones, a budget and a risk list.
Check first aid kits and emergency contact sheets each month.
Keep a list of backup carers and tell families how to reach them.
8.ex: After a month of logs, a carer sees that 6 of 8 scrapes happen at pick-up time. She changes the entry area and the scrapes fall to 2 the next month.
8.act: Run a 60-day pilot under supervision and write the review.
8.std: Task: run a pilot. Condition: 60 days under a qualified supervisor. Standard: logs are complete, risks are fixed and the review reasons from evidence.

quiz: What are four basic needs of a child?
Safety, food, rest and caring adults (also play and comfort).
Who sets child care licensing rules?
Each province or territory; check the current rule with the provincial authority.
What must you do if you suspect abuse or neglect?
Report it to the child protection authority.
Why do a daily safety walk?
To find and fix hazards before children are harmed.
What goes in an incident report?
Time, what happened, what you did and who was told.
How should you guide behaviour?
With calm, clear words and showing what to do, never hitting or shaming.
Why keep allergy information posted?
So every adult knows each child's risks.
How do you find a fee per child-day?
Costs plus target income, divided by child-days you can fill.
Should you share photos of children freely?
No; get consent first and protect privacy.
What should you do if you are unsure of a rule?
Ask the provincial authority or a licensed adviser and keep the answer in writing.
